1) a new phasing method has been developed for the analysis of multiwavelength anomalous diffraction (MAD), 2) the method is analogous to that used to analyze data in isomorphous-replacement methods, 3) it is applicable to MAD data from crystals of macromolecules, 4) the method is applicable to data from crystals of proteins, nucleic acids, and viruses, and 5) the method has been successfully used to determine the phases
the MAD phasing method is applicable to protein crystals with large unit cells and that the method provides a useful framework for combining phase information.
MAD data can be analyzed using a procedure analogous to that used in the method of multiple isomorphous-replacement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods and algorithms for solving crystal structures from diffraction data.
the development of a MAD phasing method that is applicable to the determination of protein structures.
the development of a new method of phasing protein structures by the multi-wavelength anomolous diffraction (MAD).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the method of MAD phasing, when applied to data of sufficient quality, is an efficient and reliable procedure for determining the phases of macromolecular structures, and that it should be the method of choice in all cases in which the data are of sufficient quality to allow its application.
the MAD phasing procedure presented here is a powerful tool for the analysis of MAD data.
the MAD method is a very powerful tool for the solution of the phase problem in macromolecular crystallography.

MAD data analysis is a powerful technique for solving protein crystallography, and that the MAD phasing method presented here is an efficient and accurate procedure.

the method described here is useful for the refinement of the positions of anomalous scatterers in protein structures, but is not useful for the refinement for the positions of all the atoms in the protein structure.
we have shown that the MAD phasing method can be applied successfully to a protein crystal of modest size.
